title: The Scarecrow's Wonderful Hat Parade
markdown:
Winkleberry Hollow usually moved like a cow in a green field: slow, happy, and not in a hurry to be interesting. Then a Saturday morning arrived that made Velvet the vixen twitch her nose and Muffin the mole pop from a hole with his pink snout already asking questions.

Velvet’s fur was the colour of crunchy autumn leaves. She trotted past Farmer McGregor’s big green field, stopped, blinked, and twitched again. Something was not sitting right on the skyline.

“That’s odd,” she said, voice soft as leaves on a breeze.

Muffin’s fur was as fuzzy as a dandelion puff. He wriggled out of a fresh tunnel, whiskers quivering. He liked a mystery. He was less fond of new things that arrived without knocking. “What’s odd, Velvet?”

She pointed her snout at the middle of the field. “The scarecrow is wearing a new hat.”

It was true. The tall droopy figure usually wore a faded straw hat that had grown old in public. Today he wore a knitted beanie the colour of a clear summer sky, with a yellow pom-pom bobbing as if it had somewhere to be.

Muffin squinted. “He had the straw hat yesterday. It tickled my nose when I popped up.”

Velvet’s tail swished. A puzzle, and puzzles were her favourite food after field mice she did not mention in company. “Who changes a scarecrow’s hat in the middle of the night?”

The next morning, pink and gold still wet on the horizon, they hurried back. The scarecrow stood as still as ever, button eyes on the corn. His hat had changed again. A jaunty red sailor cap sat there now, with a little white anchor that had never seen a boat.

“Oh my whiskers,” said Muffin. “It’s a hat parade.”

Velvet was already sniffing the dew around the pole. A single glossy black feather lay at the bottom, neat as a calling card. “A crow. Crows do not usually wear hats. Not even the fancy ones.”

They followed disturbed earth and a few more of those feathers away from the field, toward the Whispering Woods. An old oak held up its branches like twisty fingers. High in them sat a nest that was not only twigs and mud. Ribbons. Shiny buttons. And hats arranged along the rim as carefully as a shop window: the sky-blue beanie, the sailor cap, and a deep purple top hat tilted just so.

Leaves rustled. A sleek black crow dropped to a lower branch, one bright eye gleaming. “Who goes there, little ones?” His caw was friendlier than the stories about him.

Velvet stepped onto moss that gave under her paws. “We are Velvet and Muffin. We’ve come about the scarecrow’s hats. They seem to have disappeared.”

The crow tilted his head and chuckled, dry leaves on a path. “Ah, the hats. We do like to borrow them. Just for a little while.”

More crows swooped in: a mother looking quite grand, a father with a proud chest, and three fluffy young ones with yellow beaks still learning how to be solemn.

“Our little ones have developed excellent taste,” said the father, puffing. “They admire your scarecrow. They wanted him to wear the handsomest hats in Winkleberry Hollow.”

Muffin giggled, a bubbly sound that surprised him. “You’re decorating the nest with hats?”

“And adorning the scarecrow too,” said the mother, nudging a chick. “We do not want him bored, standing all day and night. A scarecrow should look his best. He is very important.”

Velvet found herself smiling. It was a wonderfully strange reason, and it still left a farmer in the morning with a memory that did not match the pole. “He does need to look his best. But Farmer McGregor may get confused if the hat changes every night. He may think he is forgetting what he put on.”

The crows looked at one another. They had not budgeted for the farmer. “A good point, little vixen,” said the father, ruffling. “We loved the colours. And the shapes. We had not quite thought of the man.”

Velvet thought of woods that already owned their own decorations. “What if we helped you find other lovely things for the nest? Things that belong here. And a splendid hat the scarecrow may keep, one you can all admire, so the farmer does not worry.”

The young crows chirped; their heads bobbed like the pom-pom that had started the trouble. The father ruffled again, which among crows meant a meeting was in session. “A splendid hat. And other treasures.”

They spent the rest of that Saturday collecting. Fallen leaves like tiny painted pictures. Berries that gleamed like rubies if you did not eat them first. Smooth pebbles that kept a bit of sun. For the scarecrow they found a wide-brimmed hat of the softest green moss, still damp, smelling of forest floor, and they set a single sunflower in it, golden face beaming as if it had applied for the job. The crows tied it on with sturdy vines. The smallest chick gasped. “The most splendid hat of all.”

From then on the scarecrow wore the mossy hat every day, as if it had grown there. The nest brightened with leaves and stones that did not need to be returned by dawn. Winkleberry Hollow went back to being ordinary, which was its talent. Sometimes, when the wind moved the corn, you could see the little crows on the oak, watching their friend on the pole, and if you were as nosy as Velvet you might catch the whisper: he does look rather smart today.
